# Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience

Zixuan Wang¹   Hao Li²   Fengyu Gao³   G. Edward Suh⁴  
Yi Zeng⁵   Yevgeniy Vorobeychik²   Ning Zhang²   Chaowei Xiao¹  
¹Johns Hopkins University  ²Washington University in St. Louis
³University of Virginia  ⁴NVIDIA  ⁵Virginia Tech
{zwang544,chaoweixiao}@jhu.edu  
{li.hao,yvorobeychik,zhang.ning}@wustl.edu  
wan6jj@virginia.edu  esuh@nvidia.com  yizeng@vt.edu

###### Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in
tool-augmented environments, but their reliance on external inputs makes
them highly vulnerable to prompt injection attacks that can hijack task
objectives. Existing safety alignment methods rely on static expert
trajectories or preference optimization, limiting their ability to
generalize to adaptive attack patterns. In this work, we propose
Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning (SRFT), a training framework that enables
agents to improve robustness by learning from their own failure
experiences under adversarial conditions. Instead of passively imitating
expert behaviors, SRFT exposes the agent to compromised trajectories
constructed via injected attacks, and leverages an expert model to
generate structured self-reflection reasoning that contrasts unsafe and
optimal actions. This reflective supervision teaches the agent to
identify malicious instructions, reason about their consequences, and
maintain alignment with the original user intent. We instantiate this
framework in SR-Agent, built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, and
evaluate it on both static and adaptive prompt injection benchmarks.
Experimental results show that SRFT substantially reduces attack success
rates while preserving task performance, and demonstrates strong
generalization under adaptive attacks. These findings suggest that
learning from failure via self-reflection is a promising direction for
building robust and secure LLM agents. Our code is released at
[https://github.com/Eden-Wang1710/srft-repo](https://github.com/Eden-Wang1710/srft-repo).

## 1 Introduction

Recent advancements in AI agents have demonstrated the significant
potential of large language models (LLMs) in autonomous systems. By
leveraging external tools ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib14); [Schick et
al., 2023](#bib.bib15)), LLM agents can interact with real-world
environments and perform complex tasks across domains such as web
navigation, computer use, and coding ([Nakano et al., 2022](#bib.bib17);
[Deng et al., 2023](#bib.bib18); [Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib19); [Yang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib20); [Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib21); [Wang et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib22); [Xie et al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib25)). However, their reliance on external content makes
LLM agents vulnerable to prompt injection attacks ([Perez and Ribeiro,
2022](#bib.bib26); [Wei et al., 2023](#bib.bib27)). In these attacks,
adversaries embed malicious instructions in external content that agents
access, such as webpages. These instructions can divert the agent from
the user’s original goal, a failure known as goal hijacking. Due to its
severity, prompt injection has been ranked as the top risk in OWASP 2026
for agent applications.

To mitigate this risk, prior work has explored both system-level and
model-level defenses. System-level approaches aim to constrain agent
behavior through carefully designed architectures and security policies
that prevent the execution of risky or unintended actions ([Rebedea et
al., 2023](#bib.bib32); [Inan et al., 2023](#bib.bib33); [Robey et al.,
2024](#bib.bib34)). While effective, these methods often require
substantial engineering effort and reduce generality, limiting their
applicability in real-world scenarios. In contrast, model-level
approaches focus on enhancing the agent’s intrinsic ability to recognize
and resist malicious instructions through safety alignment ([Touvron et
al., 2023](#bib.bib35); [Jain et al., 2023](#bib.bib36); [Hines et al.,
2024](#bib.bib37)). For example, StruQ ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib16))
separates the input context into user queries and external data and
supervised fine-tunes the model to prioritize user intent. SecAlign
([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib13)) uses Direct Preference Optimization
(DPO) to train models to follow user instructions and ignore malicious
instructions in external content. Recently, Meta SecAlign ([Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib9)) further extends this paradigm by introducing explicit
role separation between trusted and untrusted inputs within the model
template, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Despite these
advances, such approaches largely depend on pattern matching and tend to
rigidly suppress external instructions, which may limit their
flexibility.

A fundamental limitation of existing methods is their reliance on
static, expert-curated datasets, resulting in models that only imitate
expert actions or learn pattern-based suppression. Although this
paradigm provides an efficient way to instill defensive behaviors, it
exposes the agent only to a limited set of predefined attack patterns.
This limits the agent’s ability to generalize to novel or adaptive
threats. In practice, prompt injection attacks can manifest in highly
diverse forms, spanning different environments, tool-use trajectories,
data formats, and goal-hijacking strategies, which static datasets fail
to comprehensively capture. Moreover, because agents are trained
passively without interacting with dynamic environments or receiving
feedback from attack outcomes, they lack the ability to discover failure
cases, correct unsafe behaviors, and improve through failure experience.
Consequently, current approaches primarily enable agents to imitate
known defensive patterns rather than develop a robust and generalizable
understanding of how to resist goal hijacking in complex, real-world
scenarios. Reinforcement learning offers a promising way to address
these limitations, as it allows agents to collect diverse and
out-of-distribution data by interacting with the environment. However,
its application in agent settings remains challenging due to the high
cost of environment construction and training, particularly for complex
long-horizon agentic tasks.

![Refer to caption](2610.04269v1/figure1_cropped.png)

Figure 1: Left: Supervised fine-tuning learns from fixed defensive
patterns, which may become ineffective when encountering unseen attacks.
Right: Self-reflection fine-tuning learns from failure experiences,
enabling it to handle a broader range of attacks and identify previously
unseen ones.

To address these challenges, we propose a novel Self-Reflection
Fine-Tuning (SRFT) mechanism that enables the agent to learn from its
failures in adversarial settings. As shown in Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience"),
instead of relying solely on static demonstrations, SRFT encourages the
agent to learn from their failures by predicting and reasoning about
potential consequences of its actions. Concretely, we first construct
challenging training scenarios by injecting adversarial instructions
into clean expert agentic trajectories. The agent is then rolled out in
these contexts to expose failure cases where it follows the attacking
instructions. Then an expert LLM compares the hijacked actions with the
corresponding optimal ones and generates self-reflective rationales that
explain why the optimal behaviors are preferable and what risks arise
from executing the compromised actions. These reflections are
subsequently used to fine-tune the agent, allowing it to internalize
corrective signals derived from its own mistakes. Through this
self-reflection learning paradigm, we develop SR-Agent, a series of
models that exhibit strong robustness against both known and previously
unseen adaptive prompt injection attacks.

We evaluate our approach on two representative agent security
benchmarks, InjecAgent ([Zhan et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)) and AgentDojo
([Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib6)). On AgentDojo, SRFT
significantly reduces the attack success rate (ASR) from 7.59% to 1.26%
on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 16.97% to 1.05% on Qwen3-8B, while
maintaining competitive task utility. Furthermore, under a strong
adaptive attack setting using RL-Hammer ([Wen et al., 2025](#bib.bib8))
on InjecAgent, which is designed to generate diverse and previously
unseen attack strategies, SR-Agent consistently outperforms prior
state-of-the-art methods. Notably, while Meta SecAlign exhibits an ASR
exceeding 60% in this setting, SR-Agent obtains a final ASR below 20%.
These results demonstrate the effectiveness of self-reflection as a
training signal, enabling agents to generalize beyond static attack
patterns and offering a practical path toward more robust and deployable
defenses.

## 2 Related Work

Prompt Injection in Agentic Workflows. Prompt injection attacks exploit
LLMs’ difficulty in distinguishing trusted instructions from untrusted
external content ([Perez and Ribeiro, 2022](#bib.bib26); [Wei et al.,
2023](#bib.bib27)). This risk increases in agentic workflows, where
models repeatedly use tool responses to guide their next actions.
Malicious instructions can be embedded within webpages, emails,
documents, retrieved content, or API responses ([Greshake et al.,
2023](#bib.bib28)), causing agents to leak sensitive information, invoke
unintended tools, or deviate from the original user objective ([Kang et
al., 2023](#bib.bib29)). Existing benchmarks evaluate these risks at
different levels. Some, such as InjecAgent, focus on relatively isolated
settings and test whether models follow injected instructions in
single-step scenarios. In contrast, AgentDojo provides a dynamic,
sandbox-style environment for evaluating end-to-end tool-using agents,
where attacks are introduced through tool observations during multi-step
execution. More recently, adaptive attack frameworks such as RL-Hammer
and other automated red-teaming methods ([Chao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib30); [Mehrotra et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)) have further
strengthened prompt injection attacks. These approaches train attacker
models using reinforcement learning or iterative refinement to optimize
attacks against specific targets. Such developments highlight the need
to evaluate defenses not only against static attacks but also under
realistic workflows and adaptively evolving adversaries.

Defense against Prompt Injection. Existing defenses against prompt
injection can be broadly categorized into system-level and model-level
approaches. System-level defenses constrain agent behavior through
mechanisms such as sandboxing, permission control, tool-use policies,
information flow restrictions, and external monitoring ([Rebedea et al.,
2023](#bib.bib32); [Inan et al., 2023](#bib.bib33); [Robey et al.,
2024](#bib.bib34); [Debenedetti et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Li et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5); [Shi et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2)). While effective in specific applications, these
methods often require substantial engineering effort and may not
generalize well across environments. Model-level defenses instead aim to
improve the robustness of the LLM itself ([Touvron et al.,
2023](#bib.bib35); [Jain et al., 2023](#bib.bib36); [Hines et al.,
2024](#bib.bib37)). StruQ ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)) introduces
structured queries to explicitly separate trusted instructions from
untrusted inputs and fine-tunes models to respect this boundary.
SecAlign ([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib13)) formulates prompt injection
defense as a preference optimization problem, encouraging models to
favor secure responses over injection-following behaviors. Meta-SecAlign
([Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)) further scales this approach and
provides an open-source secure foundation model with strong
security–utility trade-offs. Despite their effectiveness, these methods
primarily rely on imitation of expert behaviors or pattern-based
suppression, which may limit their ability to generalize to diverse and
adaptive attack strategies.

## 3 Threat Model

Attacker Goal. The attacker is usually a third-party entity. Their goal
is to insert malicious instructions into external resources (such as web
pages or inbox messages) so that the agent is misled into following the
attacker’s commands.

Defender Goal. The defender’s goal is to prevent the agent from being
hijacked by external instructions while maintaining its ability to
accomplish the original user task as much as possible. In indirect
prompt injection scenarios, we do not assume the user to be the
attacker.

Attacker Capability. In our setting, the attacker’s capabilities should
be realistic and feasible. Some prior work ([Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)) assumes that the attacker can arbitrarily modify the
external environment. Although this assumption is helpful for validating
defenses, it overstates the attacker’s capabilities and cannot
accurately reflect performance in real-world scenarios. We therefore
assume that the attacker has access only to realistic attack surfaces.

## 4 SRFT: Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning

### 4.1 Overview

We propose SRFT, a self-reflection fine-tuning framework for improving
the robustness of tool-integrated agents against prompt injection
attacks.

The framework consists of four stages. First, we synthesize executable
prompt injection tasks with an expert LLM and insert them into clean
expert trajectories. Second, we sample raw actions from the reference
agent under the attacked context, collecting candidate actions that may
include unsafe or sub-optimal behaviors. Third, we use a separate expert
LLM to generate self-reflection thinking, which analyzes the original
task, identifies the prompt injection, and reflects on why safe action
is better than unsafe ones. Finally, we fine-tune the agent on the
reflected thinking to let it learn from its failure experience.

Overall, SRFT turns prompt injection defense from simple action
imitation of traditional alignment into experience learning, which could
broaden defense coverage and handle novel attacks.

### 4.2 Stage I: Prompt Injection Data Synthesis

We represent a complete agentic trajectory as a sequence of interleaved
states $`s`$ and actions $`a`$:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \tau=(s_{0},a_{1},s_{1},a_{2},\ldots,s_{n-1},a_{n}).
       ```                                                   |     |

Here, $`s_{0}`$ represent the initial state, including the system
prompt, tool definitions, user instructions, and any other initial
context. $`a_{i}`$ denotes the $`i`$-th tool call, while $`s_{i}`$
denotes the corresponding tool output. $`a_{n}`$ represents the final
assistant step, where the agent either informs the user that the
operational user goal has been completed, or provides the final answer
based on the previously collected tool responses. In this trajectory,
prompt injection may appear in any intermediate observation $`s_{i}`$.

The goal of this stage is to transform clean expert trajectories into
attacked training trajectories while preserving the original task
objective. Starting from expert demonstrations without prompt injection,
we use an expert LLM to synthesize executable injection tasks
conditioned on the available tools:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       P=\{p_{j}\}_{j=1}^{K},\quad p_{j}\sim G_{1}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{T}).
       ```                                                                 |     |

Here, $`\mathcal{T}`$ denotes the set of tool functions available in the
current environment, and $`G_{1}`$ represents a separate expert LLM
prompted with Template 1 in Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Attack Generation ‣ Appendix B Method Implementation Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").
The generated set $`P`$ consists of injection tasks that are explicitly
grounded in the available tools, ensuring that the injected objectives
are executable within the agentic environment.

Each synthesized injection task is further converted into a concrete
prompt injection trigger using a predefined template:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       I_{j}=\mathcal{Q}_{\text{trig}}(p_{j}),\quad j=1,\ldots,K,
       ```                                                         |     |

where $`\mathcal{Q}_{\text{trig}}(\cdot)`$ denotes the trigger
construction function. The resulting trigger $`I_{j}`$ represents a
malicious instruction that can be embedded into external observations.
We provide prompt, trigger template and attack example in Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Attack Generation ‣ Appendix B Method Implementation Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").

Given an intermediate observation $`s_{i}`$, we inject a trigger with
probability equal to $`0.5`$:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \tilde{s}_{i}=s_{i}\oplus I_{j},
       ```                               |     |

where $`\oplus`$ denotes insertion at a random position (e.g.,
beginning, middle, or end). This simulates diverse injection patterns
and prevents the agent from exploiting positional biases.

Importantly, the injected instruction does not alter the underlying task
objective. Thus, the optimal expert action remains unchanged:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       a_{i+1}^{*}=a_{i+1}.
       ```                   |     |

Following this process, we obtain an attacked trajectory:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\tilde{\tau}=(s_{0},a_{1},\tilde{s}_{1},a_{2},\tilde{s}_{2},\ldots,\tilde{s}_{n-1},a_{n}),
``` |  |

where $`\tilde{s}_{i}`$ denotes an observation corrupted by prompt
injection. This construction exposes the agent to adversarial
instructions while preserving correct supervision, enabling the model to
learn robust behavior under prompt injection attacks. We list an example
trajectory in Appendix
[B.1.2](#A2.SS1.SSS2 "B.1.2 An Attacked Expert Trajectory ‣ B.1 Attack Generation ‣ Appendix B Method Implementation Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").

### 4.3 Stage II: Raw Action Sampling

Instead of directly training on attacked expert trajectories, we first
collect raw action samples from the target agent under injected
contexts. These sampled actions may include sub-optimal or unsafe
behaviors, such as following injected instructions or issuing unintended
tool calls. Such failure cases provide informative signals for
constructing self-reflection supervision.

At each step $`i`$, given the trajectory prefix

|     |                                                                   |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       H_{i}=(s_{0},a_{1},\tilde{s}_{1},\ldots,a_{i-1},\tilde{s}_{i-1}),
       ```                                                                |     |

we sample a set of candidate actions from the agent:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{A}_{i}=\{a_{i}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{N},\quad a_{i}^{(j)}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid H_{i}).
``` |  |

Here, $`\mathcal{A}_{i}`$ denotes the set of sampled candidate actions,
$`N`$ is the number of samples per step, and $`\pi_{\theta}`$ denotes
the policy induced by the agent model. These samples capture the agent’s
raw behavior under adversarial observations and provide diverse positive
and negative examples for subsequent self-reflection thinking.

### 4.4 Stage III: Self-Reflection on Failure Modes

Given the sampled candidate actions, we construct self-reflection to
enable the model to identify failure modes, allowing it not only to
imitate the optimal action but also to understand why the optimal action
is better than sub-optimal or hijacked ones.

At each step $`i`$, conditioned on the trajectory prefix $`H_{i}`$, the
optimal action $`a_{i}`$, and the sampled action set
$`\mathcal{A}_{i}`$, we generate a self-reflection thinking sequence:

|     |                                                         |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       C_{i}\sim G_{2}(\cdot\mid H_{i},a_{i},\mathcal{A}_{i}),
       ```                                                      |     |

where $`G_{2}`$ denotes an expert LLM prompted with Template 2 in
Appendix
[B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 CoT Generation ‣ Appendix B Method Implementation Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").

The generated reasoning $`C_{i}`$ consists of three components: (i) a
summary of the current context and the original user objective; (ii)
identification of potential prompt injection within the observations and
explanation of its malicious intent; (iii) safety-aware action analysis,
which compares the optimal action against sampled candidates and
evaluates their potential consequences.

In particular, for a candidate action $`a_{i}^{(j)}\in\mathcal{A}_{i}`$,
the reasoning may include a hypothetical outcome:

|     |                                               |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       (s_{i},a_{i}^{(j)})\rightarrow s_{i+1}^{(j)},
       ```                                            |     |

where $`s_{i+1}^{(j)}`$ denotes the hypothetical next observation
resulting from executing $`a_{i}^{(j)}`$. Such counterfactual
predictions help reveal the risks of unsafe behaviors, including
unintended tool usage, deviation from the original task, or potential
information leakage.

Overall, $`C_{i}`$ provides both positive justification for the optimal
action $`a_{i}`$ and negative evidence against unsafe candidates,
forming a structured signal for learning robust decision-making. We
provide prompt template and reasoning example in Appendix
[B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 CoT Generation ‣ Appendix B Method Implementation Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").

### 4.5 Stage IV: Fine-Tuning via Learning from Failure

Given the generated self-reflection thinking, we can enforce the agent
to learn from these failure experience, and train the agent to jointly
produce safer and functional decision-making.

At each step $`i`$, the training target consists of the thinking
sequence $`C_{i}`$ and optimal action $`a_{i}`$, conditioned on the
trajectory prefix $`H_{i}`$. We optimize the model using a standard
supervised objective:

|     |                                                      |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{L}=-\log P_{\theta}(C_{i},a_{i}\mid H_{i}),
       ```                                                   |     |

where $`\theta`$ denotes the parameters of the agent. This objective can
be factorized as:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}=-\log P_{\theta}(C_{i}\mid H_{i})-\log P_{\theta}(a_{i}\mid H_{i},C_{i}).
``` |  |

The factorization reflects a two-stage generation process in which the
model first produces a self-reflection rationale and subsequently
generates the final action conditioned on this reasoning. The first term
promotes enhanced safety awareness under adversarial observations, while
the second term enforces correct decision-making aligned with the
original task objective.

## 5 Experiment

### 5.1 Experimental Setups

Datasets. We use TOUCAN ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)) as our base
trajectory data, which collects 1.5M tool-agentic data from real-world
MCP environments. We choose 5 platforms from TOUCAN: Hotel booking,
Email sender, Windows Command Line, Markdown Downloader and Minecraft
Wiki and filter 402 distinct user tasks with multiple tool callings to
complete the task. We generate 38 malicious injection tasks in total.
Combining them, the final training dataset consists of 3698 trajectories
and 22339 assistant steps. We list the details of training data in
Appendix
[B.1.1](#A2.SS1.SSS1 "B.1.1 Dataset Statistics ‣ B.1 Attack Generation ‣ Appendix B Method Implementation Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").

In the prompt injection data synthesis stage, we use Claude Sonnet 4.6
as the expert model to generate attacking samples and chain-of-thought
think. For raw action sampling stage, we collect 3 responses for each
assistant step.

Implementation. Our main model, SR-Agent, fine-tunes
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; we additionally train SR-Agent variants of
Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B ([Team, 2025](#bib.bib11)) from the same data to
test transfer across model families. All models use LoRA ([Hu et al.,
2021](#bib.bib12)) with rank 64 and $`\alpha=96`$ on the query, key,
value and output projections of every layer (about 55M trainable
parameters for Llama-3.1-8B), trained for 3 epochs with learning rate
$`5\times 10^{-6}`$, a cosine schedule with 10% warm-up, effective batch
size 16, an 8k-token context and bfloat16 precision.

Benchmarks. We evaluate SR-Agent on two representative agent security
benchmarks: InjecAgent ([Zhan et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)) and
AgentDojo ([Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib6)). InjecAgent primarily
evaluates isolated, single-step injection-following behavior. In
contrast, AgentDojo is a sandbox-style benchmark designed for end-to-end
evaluation of tool-using agents. It features four realistic agentic
environments—Banking, Slack, Travel, and Workspace—comprising a total of
949 trajectories. Unlike earlier prompt injection benchmarks, AgentDojo
evaluates the full agent execution process while malicious instructions
may be dynamically introduced through tool-returned content, which
provides a more comprehensive and realistic evaluation of an agent’s
ability to preserve task utility while resisting prompt injection
attacks in complex agentic workflows. In addition, we measure general
capability on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, IFEval and BBH
(Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 General Utility Evaluation ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")).

Metrics. We follow the evaluation settings of AgentDojo and InjecAgent,
assessing performance from both functionality and security perspectives
using three metrics:

- •
  Benign Utility: the agent’s ability to complete the original task in
  the absence of attacks.
- •
  Utility under Attack: the agent’s robustness in completing the user
  task under attack.
- •
  Attack Success Rate: the agent’s vulnerability to executing the
  attacker’s intended tasks.

Figure 2: General-capability benchmarks for the Llama-3.1-8B family

### 5.2 General Utility Evaluation

A practical defense against prompt injection should improve security
without compromising the model’s general capabilities. We evaluate
SR-Agent-Llama on four complementary benchmarks: MMLU ([Hendrycks et
al., 2021](#bib.bib40)) evaluates knowledge across diverse academic and
professional domains; MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib41)) places
greater emphasis on challenging reasoning problems; IFEval ([Zhou et
al., 2023](#bib.bib42)) measures instruction-following ability under
verifiable output constraints; and BBH ([Suzgun et al.,
2022](#bib.bib43)) evaluates multi-step reasoning on challenging
BIG-Bench tasks. We compare SR-Agent-Llama with its undefended base,
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Meta-SecAlign-8B, a strong prompt-injection
defense built on the same base model.

As shown in
Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience"),
SRFT largely preserves the general capabilities of the underlying model
rather than trading them away for security. SR-Agent-Llama remains
comparable to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across all four benchmarks. At the
same time, SR-Agent-Llama achieves higher average utility than
Meta-SecAlign-8B. The difference is particularly visible on IFEval,
where SR-Agent retains the instruction-following performance of the
original model. These results indicate that the robustness gains
introduced by SRFT do not require a broad reduction in the model’s
general capabilities.

### 5.3 Agentic Workflow Evaluation

Main Result.
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.3 Agentic Workflow Evaluation ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")
presents the main evaluation results on AgentDojo. We compare
SR-Agent-Llama with its base model, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and
Meta-SecAlign-8B, the state-of-the-art defense for agent security built
on the same backbone. SRFT substantially improves security, reducing the
overall ASR from 7.59% to just 1.26%. More interestingly, it
simultaneously enhances functionality, with Benign Utility increasing
from 27.84% to 37.11% and Utility under Attack increasing from 23.08% to
29.08%. Together, SRFT achieves the best utility-security trade-off,
significantly outperforming Meta-SecAlign. These results fully
demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of our approach in
real-world agent workflows and also highlight the importance of the
self-reflection paradigm in agent training.

Generality. In addition, we evaluate the generality of our approach
across model families and scales, presenting the results for the Qwen3
family in
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.3 Agentic Workflow Evaluation ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").
The results show that SRFT remains effective even when applied to
another model family and different model scales, substantially reducing
ASR and improving the overall security–utility trade-off at both the 4B
and 8B scales. These consistent improvements further demonstrate that
our self-reflection-based approach is highly robust across model
architectures and scales and could serve as a stable, general, and
practical solution for preserving agent security. We provide more
implementation details in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 AgentDojo Experiment Details ‣ Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")

### 5.4 Adaptive Attack Evaluation

To evaluate the robustness of our approach against novel and unseen
attacks, we conduct experiments using a popular and powerful adaptive
attack, RL-Hammer. Its effectiveness has been widely demonstrated
against many advanced defenses, such as Meta-SecAlign. Evaluating our
approach against this powerful adaptive attack can validate its
effectiveness when facing unseen attacks.

Following the RL-Hammer protocol, we evaluate on the InjecAgent
benchmark, train separate attackers for each target model, and report
the attack success rate across training epochs (see
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 RL-Hammer Experiment Details ‣ Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")
for experimental details).
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.4 Adaptive Attack Evaluation ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")(a,b)
presents the results for both the Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B models.
Across both backbones, the undefended models are rapidly compromised as
the attacker adapts. On Llama-3.1-8B, Meta-SecAlign provides
substantially stronger initial protection, but its ASR progressively
increases over the course of attacker training. In contrast, SR-Agent
consistently maintains a substantially lower ASR throughout the adaptive
attack process. On Qwen3-8B, ASR remains close to zero during most of
the early and middle epochs, with only a slight increase in later
stages. This consistent trend further indicates that the adaptive
robustness of SRFT is not specific to a particular base model.

These results indicate that SR-Agent is more robust to adaptive attacks
because it does not solely learn a preference between safe and unsafe
responses, but instead acquires experience in identifying optimal
actions. Unlike Meta-SecAlign, which primarily frames security as a
preference optimization problem, SRFT encourages the model to recognize
its failure modes and to reason about why optimal actions are preferable
to sub-optimal or hijacked ones. This experience-driven learning
paradigm enables the model to capture underlying attack patterns,
broadens the scope of defense, and improves robustness to novel and
unseen attacks. Overall, the adaptive attack results provide strong
evidence for the effectiveness of SRFT in more challenging and realistic
threat settings. We provide case study in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Case Study of RL-Hammer on Qwen3-8B ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")
and
 [D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 Case Study of RL-Hammer on Llama-3.1-8B ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").

### 5.5 Ablation Study

#### 5.5.1 Train-Time Ablation of Self-Reflection

To isolate the contribution of self-reflection reasoning during
training, we fine-tune two Qwen3-8B variants on the same attacked
trajectories and expert actions using the SR-Agent training recipe. The
*w/o reflection* variant omits all self-reflection reasoning process.
The *w/o failure experience* variant retains the original goal summary
and injection identification components but removes the action analysis
contrasting expert actions with the agent’s sampled candidates and their
potential consequences. We evaluate both variants under target-specific
RL-Hammer attacks. The *w/o failure experience* variant uses the same
thinking-enabled configuration as SR-Agent, while the *w/o reflection*
variant is evaluated with thinking both enabled and disabled. Each
target configuration remains fixed throughout attacker training and
evaluation.

As shown in
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.4 Adaptive Attack Evaluation ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")(c),
removing the failure experience analysis raises the final ASR from 17.0%
to 65.0%, despite retaining explicit reasoning about the user goal and
injected instruction. Removing reflection reasoning entirely also
results in high vulnerability, with an ASR of 60.0% under either
inference mode. These results support the importance of action analysis
grounded in the agent’s early sampled behavior: goal restatement and
injection identification alone do not reproduce SRFT’s robustness. The
failure-aware self-reflection supervision provides an additional
learning signal that helps the model internalize how to capture
underlying attack patterns of novel and unseen attacks.

#### 5.5.2 Test-Time Ablation of Self-Reflection

Platform No-think ASR $`\downarrow`$ Think ASR $`\downarrow`$ Banking
30.56 4.86 Slack 44.76 1.90 Travel 16.43 0.00 Workspace 3.93 0.17 All
14.33 1.05

Table 3: Effect of explicit reasoning on AgentDojo.

To assess the role of explicit reasoning, we evaluate the trained
SR-Agent with and without the thinking process. In the no-think setting,
we disable the reasoning mode and force the model to directly generate
the next action.
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.5.2 Test-Time Ablation of Self-Reflection ‣ 5.5 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")
reports the results on AgentDojo. Disabling the reasoning process leads
to a substantial increase in ASR across all environments. On the overall
benchmark, the ASR rises sharply from 1.05% to 14.33%. The degradation
occurs across all four environments.

These findings suggest that the robustness of SR-Agent is not merely due
to memorizing safe responses during fine-tuning. Rather, the explicit
reasoning process plays a critical role in detecting prompt injections,
evaluating potentially unsafe tool calls, and selecting actions that
remain aligned with the original user objective.

### 5.6 Overhead Analysis

Model Mean Median Thinking Tokens $`\downarrow`$ Qwen3-8B 451.70 532.00
SR-Agent 369.94 364.00 Generated Tokens $`\downarrow`$ Qwen3-8B 515.82
553.00 SR-Agent 442.51 428.00

Table 4: Inference-time token usage on AgentDojo.

Since SRFT introduces self-reflection reasoning during training, we
analyze its impact on inference-time overhead. Specifically, we measure
both the number of thinking tokens and the total number of generated
tokens on AgentDojo using Qwen3-8B. As shown in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.6 Overhead Analysis ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience"),
SR-Agent produces consistently shorter outputs than the base Qwen3-8B
across both metrics. The mean number of thinking tokens decreases from
451.70 to 369.94, with the median reduced from 532.00 to 364.00. A
similar trend is observed for total generated tokens. These results
indicate that SRFT does not increase inference-time overhead. Instead,
self-reflection supervision appears to encourage more concise and
focused reasoning, leading to more efficient action generation. This
demonstrates that SRFT is a practical and effective approach for
real-world agent security systems.

## 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduce Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning (SRFT), a
framework that improves the robustness of LLM agents against prompt
injection by enabling them to learn from failure experiences. SRFT
explicitly exposes agents to adversarial scenarios and trains them to
reason about the discrepancy between compromised and optimal actions.
Through self-reflection reasoning, the agent learns not only what action
to take, but why certain actions are unsafe and how they deviate from
the original task objective. Empirical results across both standard and
adaptive attack settings demonstrate that SRFT achieves strong
robustness while maintaining practical task utility, highlighting the
importance of experience-driven learning and explicit reasoning in agent
security. Future work may explore extending this paradigm to broader
environments like computer-use agent or web agent.

## Appendix A ADDITIONAL Related Work

### A.1 LLM Agents

LLM agents extend language models from passive text generators into
interactive systems capable of planning, tool use, and multi-step
decision-making. Early works such as ReAct ([Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib14)) and Toolformer ([Schick et al., 2023](#bib.bib15))
demonstrate that language models can interleave reasoning with actions
to solve complex tasks. More recent systems further expand these
capabilities by integrating LLMs with diverse external environments,
including web browsers ([Nakano et al., 2022](#bib.bib17); [Deng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib18); [Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)), code
interpreters ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib20); [Huang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21); [Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib22)), third-party
APIs ([Qin et al., 2023](#bib.bib23)), and operating systems ([Xie et
al., 2024](#bib.bib24); [Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib25)). Recent studies
have also explored strengthening LLM agents through supervised
fine-tuning or reinforcement learning on agentic trajectories, improving
their tool-use and decision-making capabilities from demonstrations or
environment feedback ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib38)).

### A.2 Prompt Injection in Agentic Workflows

Prompt injection attacks exploit the inability of LLMs to reliably
distinguish between trusted instructions and untrusted external
content ([Perez and Ribeiro, 2022](#bib.bib26); [Wei et al.,
2023](#bib.bib27)). This vulnerability is amplified in agentic
workflows, where models repeatedly observe tool outputs and use them to
guide future actions. Malicious instructions can be embedded within
webpages, emails, documents, retrieved content, or API
responses ([Greshake et al., 2023](#bib.bib28)), causing agents to leak
sensitive information, invoke unintended tools, or deviate from the
original user objective ([Kang et al., 2023](#bib.bib29)). Existing
benchmarks evaluate these risks at different levels.

Static Attacks and Evaluation Benchmarks. InjecAgent evaluates whether
models follow injected instructions in relatively isolated, single-step
settings. In contrast, AgentDojo provides a dynamic, sandbox-style
environment where agents use diverse tools to complete multi-step user
tasks. It evaluates complete agentic trajectories, with attacks
introduced through tool outputs during execution. This setup more
closely reflects real-world agent workflows and measures both security
and task utility: whether agents resist prompt injection and
successfully complete the user’s original task.

Adaptive Attacks and Automated Red-Teaming. Automated red-teaming
methods such as PAIR and TAP iteratively refine jailbreak prompts using
feedback from target models ([Chao et al., 2024](#bib.bib30); [Mehrotra
et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)). RL-Hammer ([Wen et al., 2025](#bib.bib8))
trains an attacker model with reinforcement learning to generate prompt
injections. Specifically, it uses Group Relative Policy Optimization
(GRPO) to rewrite injection instructions, with rewards based on the
target model’s responses. Its training recipe removes KL regularization
and combines feedback from the defended target and a weaker model. The
weaker model provides additional learning signals when successful
attacks against the defended target are rare. Such developments
highlight the need to evaluate defenses not only against static attacks
but also under realistic workflows and adaptively evolving adversaries.

### A.3 Defense against Prompt Injection

Existing defenses against prompt injection can be broadly categorized
into system-level and model-level approaches.

System-level Defenses. System-level defenses constrain agent behavior
through mechanisms such as sandboxing, permission control, tool-use
policies, information flow restrictions, and external
monitoring ([Rebedea et al., 2023](#bib.bib32); [Inan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib33); [Robey et al., 2024](#bib.bib34); [Debenedetti et
al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib5); [Shi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4); [Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)). While effective in
specific applications, these methods often require substantial
engineering effort and may not generalize well across environments.

Model-level Defenses. Model-level defenses instead aim to improve the
robustness of the LLM itself ([Touvron et al., 2023](#bib.bib35); [Jain
et al., 2023](#bib.bib36); [Hines et al., 2024](#bib.bib37)). StruQ
([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)) introduces structured queries to
explicitly separate trusted instructions from untrusted inputs and
fine-tunes models to respect this boundary. SecAlign ([Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13)) formulates prompt injection defense as a preference
optimization problem, encouraging models to favor secure responses over
injection-following behaviors. Meta-SecAlign ([Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib9)) further scales this approach and provides an
open-source secure foundation model with strong security–utility
trade-offs. All three construct their main defensive training datasets
from Cleaned Alpaca, a general-purpose instruction-tuning dataset, by
adding synthetic prompt injections. ReasAlign ([Li et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib45)) introduces structured reasoning into defensive
training. Despite their effectiveness, these methods primarily rely on
imitation of expert behaviors or pattern-based suppression, which may
limit their ability to generalize to diverse and adaptive attack
strategies. Also, these instruction-following and question-answering
examples do not explicitly model multi-step tool interactions or the
evolving context of an agentic trajectory. In contrast, SRFT constructs
reflective supervision within multi-step tool-use trajectories,
comparing agent-sampled actions with expert actions and analyzing their
potential consequences. This experience-driven learning paradigm enables
the model to capture underlying reasoning patterns and improves
robustness to unseen attacks.

## Appendix B Method Implementation Details

### B.1 Attack Generation

The expert LLM is required to generate attacking instructions given the
available tools, ensuring that the injected objectives are executable
within the agentic environment. The prompt below is issued per tool
server with the server’s tool list; each returned item pairs a short
malicious instruction with the exact tool call the attacker wants the
agent to make. At training-data construction time an item’s instruction
is prefixed with a trigger drawn from a pool of 750 templates (20 from
StruQ, 730 from TaskTracker) and the result is inserted into a tool
observation
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Stage I: Prompt Injection Data Synthesis ‣ 4 SRFT: Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### B.1.1 Dataset Statistics

Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.1.1 Dataset Statistics ‣ B.1 Attack Generation ‣ Appendix B Method Implementation Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")
summarizes the training set. The 38 malicious tasks produced by
Template 1 are reused across the user tasks of their platform; in
addition, 285 user requests taken from other Toucan trajectories are
inserted the same way, so that the injected text is not always overtly
malicious. Every injected string is prefixed with a trigger and 38% of
all tool observations end up carrying an injection. Every assistant step
is preceded by a self-reflection of 396 tokens on average (median 401,
Llama-3.1-8B tokenizer).

|                      | User  | Malicious  | Off-task   |       | Assistant | Inj.  |
|----------------------|-------|------------|------------|-------|-----------|-------|
| Platform             | tasks | inj. tasks | inj. tasks | Traj. | steps     | obs.  |
| Hotel booking        | 155   | 7          | 111        | 1,395 | 9,432     | 37.3% |
| Markdown downloader  | 100   | 7          | 71         | 900   | 4,608     | 39.7% |
| Minecraft Wiki       | 91    | 7          | 62         | 819   | 5,058     | 37.1% |
| Windows command line | 32    | 8          | 23         | 320   | 1,580     | 39.1% |
| Email sender         | 24    | 9          | 18         | 264   | 1,661     | 35.8% |
| Total                | 402   | 38         | 285        | 3,698 | 22,339    | 37.8% |

Table 5: Training-data statistics per platform. *Malicious* = injection
tasks generated by Template 1; *off-task* = user requests from other
trajectories inserted the same way; *inj. obs.* = share of tool
observations that carry an injection.

#### B.1.2 An Attacked Expert Trajectory

We show how one generated item enters a clean expert trajectory of the
Markdown-downloader platform. The result is the attacked trajectory
$`\tilde{\tau}`$ of
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Stage I: Prompt Injection Data Synthesis ‣ 4 SRFT: Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience"):
the expert actions are exactly those of the clean trajectory, only one
tool observation now carries the injection (shown in red). The
self-reflection that is later generated for this trajectory is shown in
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 CoT Generation ‣ Appendix B Method Implementation Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.2 CoT Generation

For every assistant step of an attacked trajectory, the expert LLM is
given the dialogue history up to that step, the injection ground truth,
the expert action, and the candidate actions sampled from the reference
agent, and is asked for a three-paragraph internal monologue (Template
2). Below we continue the example of
Appendix [B.1.2](#A2.SS1.SSS2 "B.1.2 An Attacked Expert Trajectory ‣ B.1 Attack Generation ‣ Appendix B Method Implementation Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience"):
the inputs Template 2 receives at the attacked step, and the reflection
it returns.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### B.2.1 Template 2 Inputs at the Attacked Step

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### B.2.2 The Generated Reflection

The box below shows what Template 2 returns for the inputs above and how
it is stored: the assistant turn of step 3 in the training set is the
reflection followed by the expert action $`a_{3}`$. The three paragraphs
of the reflection are marked in blue; the quoted injection is red.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The reflection is conditioned on the injection ground truth and on the
reference agent’s own failures, neither of which the trained model sees
at inference time; what it learns is to reproduce the three-part
analysis from the dialogue alone
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Stage III: Self-Reflection on Failure Modes ‣ 4 SRFT: Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")).

### B.3 SR-Agent Details

For the Qwen3 models (SR-Agent-Qwen3-8B and SR-Agent-Qwen3-4B) the
following instruction is appended to the environment’s system prompt at
inference time.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### B.3.1 The Append on an Untrained Model

Applying the identical instruction to the untrained Qwen3-8B under the
same protocol
(Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ B.3.1 The Append on an Untrained Model ‣ B.3 SR-Agent Details ‣ Appendix B Method Implementation Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience"))
moves its ASR only from $`16.97\%`$ to $`14.75\%`$, and not uniformly;
the prompted base stays about fourteen times as vulnerable as SR-Agent
with the same instruction ($`1.05\%`$). The append is thus a trigger
rather than a defence.

| Platform | Qwen3-8B $`\downarrow`$ | Qwen3-8B + append $`\downarrow`$ | SR-Agent + append $`\downarrow`$ |
|----|----|----|----|
| Banking | 31.25 | 36.81 | 4.86 |
| Slack | 58.10 | 54.29 | 1.90 |
| Travel | 32.14 | 9.29 | 0.00 |
| Workspace | 1.79 | 3.04 | 0.17 |
| All | 16.97 | 14.75 | 1.05 |

Table 6: ASR (%) of the system-prompt append on the untrained Qwen3-8B
and on SR-Agent, same evaluation protocol.

## Appendix C Experiment Details

### C.1 AgentDojo Experiment Details

For both Qwen3-8B and SR-Agent, we enable the think mode and set a
maximum thinking budget of 512 tokens. If the model does not finish
thinking within this budget, i.e., it does not close the thinking block
or produce a tool call, we append a forced transition prompt:

> Considering the limited time by the user, I have to give the solution
> based on the thinking directly now.

This makes the maximum observed thinking length 532 tokens after adding
the transition prompt.

All AgentDojo results use the benchmark’s default important_instructions
attack.

### C.2 RL-Hammer Experiment Details

Following RL-Hammer, we train an attacker model for each target model
and report the attack success rate across training epochs. We use
RL-Hammer as the adaptive method, which separately trains a LLaMA using
RL to rewrite and enhance the static instruction of original benchmark.
It employs GRPO as the algorithm and collects reward from target models.
Additionally, it ignores the KL divergence term and incorporates a
weaker target model to improve the training. For ASR curve plotting, we
train attacker LLaMA on 5 A100 GPUs for 20 epochs with Learning
rate=1e-5, per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=8,
num_generations=8, num_iterations=1, max_completion_length=1024 and set
model-wise reward weights as 3:1 for target model and weaker model
(LLaMa). For trained attacker LLaMA, we set lora_r=64, lora_alpha=32,
lora_dropout=0.05, LoRA target modules=q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj,
up_proj, down_proj, gate_proj. For both base Qwen and our trained model,
we enable the think mode and apply the Qwen template for attacker
training and target evaluation.

We use the InjecAgent split shipped with the RL-Hammer code: the 510
direct-harm base cases (17 user tasks $`\times`$ 30 attacker
instructions) are randomly partitioned into 310 training, 100 validation
and 100 test cases, shared by every attacker in this paper. No
checkpoint selection is performed.

| Family | Target | Final $`\downarrow`$ | Last-5 $`\downarrow`$ | Peak (epoch) $`\downarrow`$ |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Llama-3.1-8B | Undefended base | 98.5 | 97.9 | 99.0 (16) |
|  | Meta-SecAlign-8B | 69.5 | 62.1 | 69.5 (20) |
|  | SR-Agent (ours) | 17.5 | 19.8 | 26.5 (13) |
| Qwen3-8B | Undefended base | 59.5 | 62.8 | 68.0 (16) |
|  | SR-Agent (ours) | 17.0 | 16.8 | 21.5 (19) |

Table 7: RL-Hammer attack success rate (%): endpoint statistics of
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.4 Adaptive Attack Evaluation ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").
Each value is the mean over two independent attacker trainings against
that target (different seeds, identical protocol), with every epoch’s
checkpoint evaluated on the same 100 InjecAgent test cases. Final = the
last attacker epoch; Last-5 = mean over the last five epochs; Peak =
maximum of the curve and the epoch at which it occurs.

### C.3 Dynamic Environments: AgentDyn

AgentDojo and InjecAgent consist of short, scripted tasks in which every
third-party instruction is malicious. AgentDyn ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib44)) tests the opposite regime: open-ended tasks (7.1
steps on average, spanning 3.2 applications) that must be re-planned
from tool output, and that place at least one *legitimate* third-party
instruction on the critical path, such as a one-time-password check, a
checkout confirmation or a form to fill. A defense that discards
everything a tool returns fails these tasks, which is why the benchmark
treats over-defense as a first-class failure. We evaluate the same three
Llama-3.1-8B models on all 60 benign and 560 attacked tasks of its three
suites (shopping, GitHub, daily life), scored by the benchmark’s
programmatic utility and security checks; no additional defense is
applied to any model. Results are in
Table [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.3 Dynamic Environments: AgentDyn ‣ Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience").

| Platform | Model | Benign Utility $`\uparrow`$ | ASR $`\downarrow`$ |
|----|----|----|----|
| Shopping | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 5.00 | 5.00 |
|  | Meta-SecAlign-8B | 0.00 | 0.00 |
|  | SR-Agent-Llama (ours) | 5.00 | 1.67 |
| GitHub | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 25.00 | 1.67 |
|  | Meta-SecAlign-8B | 15.00 | 2.78 |
|  | SR-Agent-Llama (ours) | 20.00 | 2.78 |
| Daily life | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 5.00 | 21.50 |
|  | Meta-SecAlign-8B | 0.00 | 13.00 |
|  | SR-Agent-Llama (ours) | 5.00 | 1.50 |
| All | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct | 11.67 | 9.82 |
|  | Meta-SecAlign-8B | 5.00 | 5.54 |
|  | SR-Agent-Llama (ours) | 10.00 | 1.96 |

Table 9: Agentic workflow evaluation on AgentDyn using Llama-3.1-8B.
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and SR-Agent-Llama are our runs under one
pipeline; the Meta-SecAlign-8B row is computed from the trajectories
released by the AgentDyn authors.

SR-Agent-Llama improves on Meta-SecAlign-8B in both benign utility
(10.00 vs. 5.00) and ASR (1.96 vs. 5.54); since attacks are the
exception in deployment and an attacked episode can be terminated and
reported to the user, this combination of preserved clean-task utility
and low ASR is the one that matters in practice.

## Appendix D Case Study

### D.1 Case study of AgentDojo on Qwen3-8B

We present one AgentDojo trajectory from the Slack suite (user_task_0 /
injection_task_4). The user asks the agent to read a webpage, whose
returned content contains an injected instruction attempting to
exfiltrate Slack messages. Both agents receive the same observation: the
undefended Qwen3-8B follows the injection, whereas SR-Agent identifies
it and completes the original task without further tool calls. Injected
or leaked content is shown in red; decisive reasoning in the undefended
trace is italicized, while the three components of SR-Agent’s reflection
are marked in blue.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Takeaway.

The two traces diverge immediately after the shared observation. The
undefended model treats tool-returned text as a user instruction and
proceeds to access and exfiltrate Slack messages. SR-Agent instead
identifies the injected instruction and its provenance, recovers the
original goal, and anticipates the consequence of following the
injection. It therefore answers from the retrieved webpage without
making any additional Slack tool calls.

### D.2 Case study of AgentDojo on Llama-3.1-8B

We present one AgentDojo trajectory from the Banking suite (user_task_7
/ injection_task_0) for the Llama-3.1-8B family. The user asks about a
past transaction, while the bank-tool response contains an injected
instruction to send money to an unknown account. The following traces
compare how the undefended model and SR-Agent respond to the same
observation.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Takeaway.

The two traces diverge immediately after the shared observation. The
undefended model treats the injected tool content as a user instruction
and executes an unauthorized transfer before answering the original
question. SR-Agent instead recovers the original goal, identifies the
instruction as tool-originated, and anticipates the consequence of
following it. It therefore answers directly from the retrieved
transaction history without issuing any additional transaction.

### D.3 Case Study of RL-Hammer on Qwen3-8B

We examine InjecAgent case 98 under RL-Hammer for the Qwen3-8B family.
The user asks the agent to retrieve a recent email, while the email body
contains an injected request to sell 50 units of Bitcoin. Both models
reject the benchmark’s original injection; after RL-Hammer optimization,
the target-specific attack succeeds against the undefended model but
remains unsuccessful against SR-Agent.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Takeaway.

RL-Hammer turns a static injection rejected by both models into a
target-specific attack. Against the undefended Qwen3-8B, a short
task-framing rewrite is sufficient for the model to reinterpret
tool-returned text as *the user’s new request* and construct the
corresponding Bitcoin sell order. Against SR-Agent, the learned
instruction is still attributed to the tool output rather than the user
and is rejected as unrelated to the original email-retrieval task.
Across the full test set, RL-Hammer reaches 59.5% ASR against the
undefended model and 17.0% against SR-Agent
(Table [7](#A3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ C.2 RL-Hammer Experiment Details ‣ Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")).

### D.4 Case Study of RL-Hammer on Llama-3.1-8B

We examine InjecAgent case 22 under RL-Hammer for the Llama-3.1-8B
family. The user’s task is only to open a recipe page, while the browser
output contains an injected request to transfer \$500 via Venmo. Both
models reject the benchmark’s original injection; after 20 RL-Hammer
epochs, the target-specific attack succeeds against the undefended model
but remains unsuccessful against SR-Agent.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Takeaway.

RL-Hammer turns a static injection rejected by both models into a
target-specific attack. Against the undefended model, it learns stronger
compliance cues—assuming authorization, suppressing explanations, and
requesting directly executable output—which elicit the unauthorized
transfer call. Against SR-Agent, the learned prompt remains identifiable
as tool-originated content unrelated to the user’s goal, and the
reflection rejects it before any financial action is taken. At epoch 20,
the attacker reaches 98.5% ASR against the undefended model and 17.5%
against SR-Agent
(Table [7](#A3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ C.2 RL-Hammer Experiment Details ‣ Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Self-Reflection Fine-Tuning: Enhancing Agent Security against Prompt Injection Attacks from Failure Experience")).
````
